name: Jeff Nippard
who: Natural bodybuilder and YouTuber who turns exercise-science studies into structured hypertrophy and strength programs.
why: The reference standard for evidence-based lifting content; his myth-busting videos and programs set the tone the whole segment is measured against.
takeaway: Before adopting any training trend, ask what the studies actually measured — copy the habit of checking sources.

name: Dr. Mike Israetel
who: Sport scientist and co-founder of Renaissance Periodization (RP), known for periodization science and blunt on-camera debates.
why: RP's app and templates put periodization science in front of a mass audience; his channel and clips generate outsized engagement and debate.
takeaway: Base your training on periodization principles, not gut feel, and be ready to explain the reasoning.

name: Layne Norton
who: PhD in nutritional sciences, pro natural bodybuilder and powerlifter, runs Bio Layne coaching and the Carbon Diet Coach app.
why: One of the most credentialed nutrition scientists in fitness media; rigorous myth-debunking backed by a competitive record and a PhD.
takeaway: Pair your credentials with real competitive results — expertise lands harder when you've actually done the thing.

name: Jeff Cavaliere
who: Physical therapist and former MLB strength coach behind ATHLEAN-X, the largest science-based training channel on YouTube.
why: 14M+ YouTube subscribers make him the biggest single reach in this segment; his corrective-training, fix-your-form format is widely copied.
takeaway: Diagnose the root cause of an ache before treating the symptom — fix form, not just discomfort.

name: Andrew Huberman
who: Stanford neuroscientist and host of the Huberman Lab podcast, with recurring episodes on resistance training, recovery and VO2 max protocols.
why: His training and recovery protocol episodes move millions to change their routines overnight, the exact amplifier effect this segment is built to capture.
takeaway: Explain the mechanism behind a protocol, not just the protocol — understanding why helps people actually stick with it.

name: Peter Attia
who: Physician focused on longevity medicine and host of The Drive podcast, a strong advocate for strength and VO2 max training as lifespan medicine.
why: Popularized the idea of training for a 'Centenarian Decathlon' among a mainstream, affluent audience, pulling fitness science into longevity media.
takeaway: Train for the decades ahead, not just this season — frame fitness as a long-term investment.

name: Thomas DeLauer
who: Former bodybuilder turned science communicator covering fat loss, fasting and metabolic health.
why: One of the earliest YouTubers to build a channel purely on translating studies into practical diet and fasting protocols.
takeaway: Translate research studies into plain, practical protocols people can actually follow.

name: Eugene Teo
who: Natural bodybuilding coach and YouTuber known for minimalist, sustainable training templates grounded in research.
why: Represents the calm, low-hype wing of evidence-based lifting, popular with viewers fatigued by extreme claims.
takeaway: Favor a calm, minimalist training template over hype — sustainability beats big claims for most people.

name: Menno Henselmans
who: Evidence-based personal trainer and researcher who runs Bayesian Bodybuilding and regularly critiques published hypertrophy studies.
why: Among the most technically respected voices in evidence-based coaching, cited by peer coaches more than by mass audience size.
takeaway: Critique published research directly — respect from peer coaches matters as much as audience size.

name: Mind Pump
who: Three-host fitness media company (Sal Di Stefano, Adam Schafer, Justin Andrews) behind the 'Raw Fitness Truth' podcast and MAPS training programs.
why: The longest-running mainstream fitness podcast, with a large, loyal, purchase-ready audience and a real coaching-programs business behind it.
takeaway: Build an audience that trusts you enough to buy your program, not just watch your content.

name: Stan Efferding
who: Pro bodybuilder and powerlifter, creator of the Vertical Diet, coaches elite strength and physique athletes.
why: A rare crossover between an elite competitive record in two sports and real nutrition-coaching credibility.
takeaway: Pair a simple, repeatable diet system with real competitive results before coaching others on it.

name: Squat University
who: Aaron Horschig, physical therapist and strength coach, built Squat University on lift-specific biomechanics and injury-prevention content.
why: The go-to reference for lifters diagnosing pain and technique flaws; his format has been widely copied by other PT-creators.
takeaway: Diagnose your own lifting pain before pushing through it — treat technique flaws as injury prevention.

name: Knees Over Toes Guy
who: Ben Patrick, former basketball player turned knee-rehab specialist, creator of the ATG (Athletic Truth Group) training system.
why: Reframed how lifters and rehab clients think about knee health; the ATG split squat became a global gym staple in a few years.
takeaway: Question standard advice about an injury-prone area — a fresh rehab approach can become a global habit.

name: Alan Thrall
who: Powerlifting gym owner and coach (Untamed Strength) known for barbell-technique breakdowns and gym-culture commentary.
why: A bridge between old-school strength coaching and modern YouTube fitness media, respected in both worlds.
takeaway: Bridge old-school gym coaching with modern video breakdowns of barbell technique.

name: Mark Rippetoe
who: Strength coach and author of 'Starting Strength,' the foundational modern barbell-training text.
why: Nearly every other strength coach on this list cites his programming; the Starting Strength template is still the default beginner program decades on.
takeaway: Write your training method down clearly enough that beginners can follow it without you.

name: Meg Squats
who: Meg Gallagher, competitive powerlifter and coach, YouTuber covering training logs, form checks and women's strength content.
why: One of the most visible women in barbell-strength media, credited with helping grow the female powerlifting audience.
takeaway: Post your own training logs and form checks openly to grow your niche's audience.

name: Greg Nuckols
who: Powerlifter and researcher, co-founder of Stronger By Science, publishing deep-dive literature reviews on training and nutrition.
why: The most cited 'read the papers so you don't have to' resource in the segment, shaping how other creators talk about the evidence.
takeaway: Read the primary research yourself and cite it — sourced claims beat unfounded ones.

name: Bryan Johnson
who: Tech entrepreneur running the 'Don't Die' Blueprint longevity protocol on himself, publishing exhaustive personal training and biomarker data.
why: Turned his own body into a public longevity experiment; Blueprint training and diet updates regularly go viral well outside fitness media.
takeaway: Track and publish your own detailed biomarker data — transparency about your own body drives interest.

name: Dan John
who: Veteran strength coach, author and lecturer known for simple, durable training philosophy ('Easy Strength').
why: A coach's coach: decades of influence on how other strength coaches teach and write, measured more in citations than followers.
reach: IG ~80K, wider reach via books and seminars (approx 2026)
takeaway: Aim to influence how other coaches teach, not just how many people follow you directly.

name: Kelly Starrett
who: Physical therapist and mobility coach, co-founder of The Ready State (formerly MobilityWOD), author of 'Becoming a Supple Leopard.'
why: Mainstreamed mobility work as a training pillar; his framework is now standard vocabulary in CrossFit and strength gyms.
takeaway: Treat mobility work as a training pillar, not an afterthought before or after lifting.

name: Dr. Stuart McGill
who: Retired professor of spine biomechanics, the most-cited researcher on low-back injury and the 'McGill Big 3' core-training protocol.
why: The scientific backbone cited by nearly every strength coach on spine safety; low social reach but outsized academic and coaching-world credibility.
reach: IG ~60K, cited across tens of thousands of academic and coaching sources (approx 2026)
takeaway: Build credibility through citations and research, not social reach — the right audience will still find you.

name: Dr. Gabrielle Lyon
who: Physician specializing in 'muscle-centric medicine,' podcast host and advocate for protein intake and resistance training as preventive medicine.
why: A fast-growing crossover figure connecting clinical medicine to strength-training messaging for a mainstream health audience.
takeaway: Frame resistance training and protein intake as preventive medicine, not just aesthetics.

name: Rhonda Patrick
who: Biomedical scientist and host of FoundMyFitness, covering nutrition, exercise physiology and longevity research in technical depth.
why: Trusted by both hardcore researchers and mainstream health podcasters for accurate deep dives that regularly feature exercise-science protocols.
takeaway: Go deep on technical detail — accuracy earns trust from experts and mainstream audiences at once.
